title: Fable 5.2 Is the Best AI Ever. So Why Am I Not Switching Yet?
dek: Anthropic's Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 top nearly every benchmark ever run, solve open science problems and build an operating system from scratch. Yet the most common early reaction is uncertainty about when to reach for it over Opus 5.5, which raises a bigger question about what frontier capability is now actually for.

oneIdea.headline: The best model ever is a spiky one, and it only pays off if you get more ambitious.
oneIdea.summary: Fable 5.2 is easy to call the most powerful model that has ever existed. It leads in coding, science, cyber and robotics, and it nearly doubles the best score on real-world contractor tasks. It is also expensive, token-hungry and, for most everyday work, no better than Opus 5.5. Its failures are subtle ones of taste and judgment: it doesn't know what humans find interesting, and it doesn't notice when its own work is a slog. The upshot is that this is opportunity AI, not efficiency AI. It is a model for whole projects and for things that weren't possible before, like complete software, live agentic video and playable games. And at this capability level, figuring out what a new model is really for takes weeks, not hours.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A better model will not make a better scribe overnight
items.body: By the host's own account the new model is no better than its cheaper sibling for most everyday work, and costs more per task. Summarising a consultation is everyday work. If a scribe supplier announces an upgrade to the newest model, ask what measurably improved in their own testing, and whether the price changes.

items.title: The failure to watch for has changed
items.body: Ethan Mollick's observation is that the errors are no longer invented facts but poor judgement: work that is too long, and no sense of when it is not good enough. In a clinical note that means plausible, accurate and bloated, with the important line buried. Reading the note critically matters more, not less, and brevity is worth specifying.

items.title: Science claims are the vendor's, and early
items.body: The gene therapy and protein design results come from Anthropic's own launch material and have not been independently replicated or peer reviewed. They are interesting for research, and irrelevant to prescribing for now. Ed Zitron has published nothing on this release, so there is no opposing source; the scepticism here is mine.

headlines.headline: Fable 5.2 lifts the bar across nearly every category
headlines.summary: Fable 5.2 leads the field on the main benchmarks. On Frontier Code it is four points ahead of GPT-6 Astra and three and a half ahead of Opus 5.5. On Terminal Bench Science it is a full six points ahead of GPT-6 Astra. On cybersecurity, Mythos 5.2 beats the previous leader by about 10 percentage points in each case.

headlines.headline: Anthropic adds robotics and protein design to the scorecard
headlines.summary: Anthropic published non-standard benchmarks for emerging capabilities. Fable 5.2 scored 64.9% on RoboDojo Sim, 25 points above Opus 5.5, whose own score was already a breakout result. Mythos 5.2 hit 85.1% on protein design, six points above Mythos 5.1.

headlines.headline: Agentic knowledge work is the one complicated result
headlines.summary: On one agentic knowledge-work benchmark, Fable 5.2 completed about five points more tasks than Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Carbon. But its ELO score was lower than Opus 5.5's. It finishes more work without necessarily doing that work better than its smaller stablemate.

headlines.headline: One model generation doubled the real-world labor score
headlines.summary: On the Remote Labor Index, which uses real contractor projects, Fable 5.2 scored 41.3%. That nearly doubles Opus 5.5's 21%, and a year ago the best agent managed 2.5%. Obsolete author Garrison Lovely called it by far the most alarming score: still only a leading indicator, but a reminder of how fast change comes under exponential growth.

headlines.headline: Fable 5.2 takes the top three spots on Artificial Analysis
headlines.summary: At max effort it scored 65, five points ahead of Gemini Carbon, six ahead of Opus 5.5 and eight ahead of GPT-6 Astra. The extra-high and high settings both scored 62, filling the next two spots. Gains came mostly from science, knowledge and coding; agentic knowledge work and terminal coding sometimes only reached Opus 5.5 levels.

headlines.headline: Cheaper per token, still very expensive per task
headlines.summary: Anthropic cut Fable's per-token prices by 20%, to $8 input and $40 output per million. But at max effort it costs $26.54 per task across the AA suite: more than double Fable 5.1, 2.6× Opus 5.5 and over 4× GPT-6 Astra. Dropping to high effort brings that to $9.08, 10% cheaper than Opus 5.5 on max.

headlines.headline: Anthropic says max effort is not for everyday use
headlines.summary: Anthropic's guidance: medium is the default, high is enough for everyday coding, and extra high is for long-running agentic work with measurable outcomes. Max is for finding the ceiling. Early tester Matt Schumer argues even low covers most tasks, so real-world costs may look better than the headline numbers.

headlines.headline: Anthropic reserves Fable for the jobs other models can't do
headlines.summary: Claude writes 90% of Anthropic's code changes under human supervision. Fable 5.2 is brought in for stubborn bugs, performance work and high-value projects that would otherwise be too slow or costly, such as migrating a critical production service from Python to Rust. That may be good guidance for everyone else too.

headlines.headline: Fable 5.2 built a bootable operating system from an empty folder
headlines.summary: Over eight days, the model coordinated more than 1,000 sub-agents to write, test and review an OS. It boots on a laptop and has its own core, drivers, file storage, windows, a login screen, an installer and built-in Claude. Theo's reaction, "Yeah, and?", shows how quickly we're getting desensitized.

headlines.headline: Black holes, gene therapy and Fermat's Last Theorem
headlines.summary: Fable 5.2 solved two open theoretical-physics problems about black holes and accurately modeled 28 of 34 gene-therapy capsids. It also fully formalized Fermat's Last Theorem into a machine-readable proof in 30 hours with 1,000 agents; Opus 5.5 stalled 26% of the way through after 18 hours. NLW doesn't think the heavy science emphasis is accidental.

headlines.headline: A general model is beating purpose-built robot drivers
headlines.summary: In Anthropic's demo, Fable 5.2 piloted a pair of robotic arms, including on tasks it was never explicitly trained for. It outperformed most models designed specifically to drive robotic arms, which suggests the bitter lesson applies to advanced robotics too.

headlines.headline: Testers say: run a security audit with Fable 5.2
headlines.summary: Fitting Mythos's origin story, testers found the commercial model very strong on security. One found 10+ severe vulnerabilities, created earlier by Opus 5.5, without even asking. On Pavel Hurin's bug hunt bench, Fable found 58 of 105 planted bugs. Most top models find 40–45, and Sonnet 5.5 Max found 51 using twice as many turns at higher cost.

headlines.headline: A full 60-second ad, live, in a single shot
headlines.summary: Riley Brown had Fable 5.2 create a 60-second ad for itself live on stream, in one shot, with zoomed-in visuals, artistic shots and realistic lighting and physics. Even Claude Code creator Boris Cherny said "Whoa." NLW sees it as more evidence that agentic video is real.

headlines.headline: Every says professionals can now build production tools without reading code
headlines.summary: Every's review, "Fable 5.2 is a paradigm shift if you know what to do with it," describes a teammate building a working video editor that combines Premiere, After Effects and Ableton-style mixing with an AI agent. Their claim: Opus 5.5 keeps you in the loop, but Fable 5.2 "can take the whole product." That reopens the SaaSpocalypse question many had settled in favor of buying over building.

headlines.headline: Earlier models started projects; Fable finishes them
headlines.summary: NLW had the same experience with the original Fable 5. Earlier models let him start lots of projects, but Fable actually completed them. He rebuilt the AI Daily Brief website and extraction pipeline in the 48 hours he had access, and barely touched it during the shutdown.

headlines.headline: For most tasks, even fans say to use Opus 5.5
headlines.summary: Every's Dan Shipper called it "a spiky kind of nuts." Some tasks will blow your mind like nothing before. For everything else it's sort of normal, and Opus 5.5 is the better choice.

headlines.headline: Knowing when your own work is not good enough is a large part of what makes someone an expert, and it's the part Fable does least reliably.
headlines.summary: In "Fable 5.2 and Jagged AGI," Mollick calls the model almost AGI. Its failures have changed: no longer made-up facts but a joyless course, a 182-page paper and creative work buried in rules. Its critics and fact-checkers caught errors but never asked whether the work was too long or no fun.

headlines.headline: Fable doesn't know what humans find impressive
headlines.summary: Asked in the regular Claude interface to show off its capabilities, Fable made things that are hard to make but easy to check. These included a sentence that counts its own letters, music that harmonizes when played backwards, and a hand-built QR code. NLW found them underwhelming, since most people can't tell why they're hard. In Claude Code, it produced a far more interesting three-minute film generated entirely in the browser.

headlines.headline: Same prompt, eerily similar output, down to a hidden acrostic
headlines.summary: NLW's coding-harness result closely matched what Ethan Mollick got from nearly the same prompt, right down to the twist ending. In both, the first letters of the script's sentences spelled a hidden message. Mollick's spelled his blog name; NLW's spelled the prompt's last line, "Be amazingly clever about this."

headlines.headline: Its first episode pitch was "unfathomably boring"
headlines.summary: Asked for an impressive, data-driven AI Daily Brief episode, Fable proposed timing every AI launch from announcement to availability. It found a real gap in the coverage but couldn't tell that nobody cares. Its backup idea, grading AI predictions that have come due, worked better, but NLW thinks Opus 5.5 would have done roughly as well.

headlines.headline: Opportunity AI: should you make a game instead of a deck?
headlines.summary: Fable 5.2 asks users to do things that weren't possible before, not just to improve existing work. Its game-building looks like a real step: testers say it handles actual game mechanics, not just good-looking shells. Anthropic's Sholto Douglas called it the first model to pass his bar for "seriously fun and beautiful games." NLW wonders whether games become a new medium for personal and professional work.

headlines.headline: The top critique: for most work it's just more annoying than Opus 5.5
headlines.summary: Skeptics call Fable models stubborn, heavy on guardrails, short on taste, expensive and token-hungry. Some argue that's why this is 5.2 and not 5.5: no Opus-5-to-5.5-style leap. Within an hour, Theo was already struggling to decide which model to use.

headlines.headline: Give it the whole project, and tell it the code is its own
headlines.summary:
Anthropic's Alex Albert advises:
- Ask what's wrong with your idea before it builds anything.
- Set approval points up front, such as before deleting things, and make clear the rest is its call.
- Start on medium or high effort.
- Hand it a whole project and let it run for hours.
Anthropic's updated prompting guide adds that when told the codebase is its own, the model merges duplicate code and fixes nearby problems instead of just reporting them.

headlines.headline: New models now take weeks, not hours, to understand
headlines.summary: Even with Opus 5.5, it took three or four weeks for people to start understanding what made it different. NLW suspects Fable 5.2 has something similar in it, but finding it will take experimentation.
